subject: biology
title: B4.2 Ecological niches
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: B4.2 Ecological niches — IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025), topic B4.2.
meta_desc: IB DP Biology practice covering B4.2 Ecological niches, guide topic B4.2.
final_note: You worked through B4.2 Ecological niches — 13 guide statements.

concepts.def: The role of a species in an ecosystem: the full set of biotic and abiotic interactions that influence its growth, survival and reproduction, including how it obtains food, what feeds on it, the other species it competes or cooperates with, and the range of abiotic conditions it tolerates. A niche is a role, not a place.

An interaction between a species and other living organisms that influences its growth, survival or reproduction, for example feeding on prey, being eaten by predators, competing for resources, being infected by pathogens, or pollination. Biotic interactions are part of a species' niche.

An interaction between a species and the non-living components of its environment, such as temperature, light intensity, water availability, oxygen concentration, pH and salinity. The range of each abiotic factor a species can tolerate is part of its niche.
An organism that can grow only where oxygen gas is absent from its environment; oxygen is toxic to it, so it cannot tolerate aerobic conditions.

An organism that tolerates both the presence and the absence of oxygen gas: it uses oxygen for aerobic cell respiration when oxygen is available, and survives by anaerobic cell respiration when it is not.
An organism that requires oxygen gas in its environment and can grow only in aerobic conditions, because it depends on aerobic cell respiration.

An organism that synthesizes its own carbon compounds from simple inorganic substances such as carbon dioxide and water, using an external energy source. Plants, algae and photosynthetic prokaryotes are autotrophs that use light energy.

concepts.term: Photosynthesis as a mode of nutrition
concepts.def: The autotrophic mode of nutrition in which light energy is used to synthesize carbon compounds from carbon dioxide and water. It is the mode of nutrition of plants, of algae and of several groups of photosynthetic prokaryotes; the prokaryotes do this without chloroplasts.

An organism that obtains carbon compounds from other organisms, living or dead, rather than synthesizing them from inorganic substances. All animals are heterotrophic, as are fungi and many prokaryotes and protists.

The heterotrophic mode of nutrition used by animals, in which food is ingested (taken into the body), digested internally into small molecules, absorbed across the gut wall into the body and then assimilated into the organism's own tissues.

The final stage of holozoic nutrition, in which absorbed products of digestion, such as amino acids and monosaccharides, are taken up by cells and used to build the organism's own molecules and tissues. Assimilation is distinct from absorption, which is the passage of the products across the gut wall.

An organism that uses both autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition, for example a protist that photosynthesizes and also ingests or absorbs carbon compounds from other organisms. Euglena is a well-known freshwater example, and many mixotrophic species are part of oceanic plankton.

An obligate mixotroph must use both autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition, because neither mode alone can sustain it. A facultative mixotroph can survive using one mode alone but uses the other when it is advantageous, for example photosynthesizing in the light and feeding heterotrophically in the dark.

An organism that obtains carbon compounds from dead organic matter by secreting digestive enzymes onto it and absorbing the products of this external digestion. Saprotrophic nutrition is found in some fungi and bacteria.

A term that can be applied to fungi and bacteria with saprotrophic nutrition, because their external digestion of dead organic matter breaks it down and releases elements for recycling in the ecosystem.
One of the three domains of life, alongside Bacteria and Eukaryota. Archaea are prokaryotes but are a separate domain from bacteria, and as a group they are metabolically very diverse.

Different archaea obtain the energy needed for ATP production in one of three ways: from light, from the oxidation of inorganic chemicals, or from the oxidation of carbon compounds obtained from other organisms.

The number, type, size and arrangement of an animal's teeth. In hominids, large flat molars with thick enamel and a massive jaw with large chewing-muscle attachments indicate a herbivorous diet of tough plant material, whereas relatively small, unspecialised teeth with reduced canines indicate an omnivorous diet.

Using an established theory to reach a conclusion about a case that cannot be observed directly. Observation of living mammals produced theories relating dentition to herbivorous or carnivorous diets; applying these theories to fossil skulls allows the diets of extinct hominids to be deduced.

Adaptations of leaf-eating insects for feeding on plants. Chewing mouthparts, as in caterpillars and grasshoppers, are mandibles that bite off and grind pieces of leaf. Piercing mouthparts, as in aphids, are needle-like stylets that penetrate the leaf to reach the sap.

Toxic substances produced by plants in seeds and leaves that are not part of the plant's basic metabolism but deter, poison or harm herbivores that eat them. Together with physical structures such as thorns, they are plant adaptations for resisting herbivory.

A metabolic adaptation of some herbivores that allows them to eat plants containing toxic secondary compounds: enzymes, in the liver for example, chemically break the toxins down into harmless products that can be excreted.

Chemical, physical and behavioural features that help a predator to find, catch and kill prey, for example venom (chemical), sharp teeth, claws, acute senses or speed (physical), and hunting in groups, ambushing or stalking (behavioural).

Chemical, physical and behavioural features that help a prey animal to resist predation, for example distasteful or poisonous secretions (chemical), camouflage, shells, spines or speed (physical), and living in groups, being active at night or freezing when threatened (behavioural).

A woody climbing plant rooted in the forest soil that uses the trunks and branches of trees for support, so that it reaches the light of the canopy without producing a thick self-supporting trunk of its own.

A plant that grows on the branches of a tree, high in the forest where light is available, without roots in the soil. An epiphyte uses the tree only for support and obtains water and minerals from rain and debris; it does not take carbon compounds from the tree.

A plant, such as a strangler fig, that germinates from a seed deposited on a branch high in a tree and grows roots down the trunk to the soil. As the roots thicken and fuse around the trunk and its own leaves shade the host, the host tree may die, leaving the strangler standing in its place.

The ability of shrubs and herbs on the forest floor to photosynthesize and grow at the low light intensities that reach beneath the canopy, so that they can complete their life cycle without reaching the canopy themselves.
The potential niche of a species: the full range of conditions and resources it could use, based on its adaptations and tolerance limits, in the absence of competition from other species.

The actual extent of a species' niche when it is in competition with other species. The realized niche is the part of the fundamental niche that the species actually occupies; it can be no larger than the fundamental niche.

The principle that two species cannot indefinitely occupy the same niche in the same place: if their niches overlap completely, one species uses the shared resources more effectively and the other is eliminated from that area.

When the fundamental niches of two species overlap, competition has two possible outcomes: one species is eliminated from the area, or both species are restricted to a part of their fundamental niche, so that each occupies a realized niche that is unique to it.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the ecological niche of a species?
options: The role of the species in its ecosystem, including its biotic and abiotic interactions
The place where the species lives, described by its location and ecosystem type
The position of the species in a food chain, defined by the food it eats
The interactions of the species with other organisms, leaving out abiotic factors
mcqs.specStatementText: Niche is a role, not a place
mcqs.explain: This is the guide's definition. A niche is a role, described by the biotic and abiotic interactions that influence the species' growth, survival and reproduction, including how it obtains food.
rationales: This is the guide's definition. A niche is a role, described by the biotic and abiotic interactions that influence the species' growth, survival and reproduction, including how it obtains food.
A student who equates niche with habitat picks this. The place in which a species lives is its habitat; the niche is what the species does in that place.
A student who thinks a niche is just a trophic level picks this. Obtaining food is one part of the niche, but predators, competitors and abiotic tolerances are also part of it.
A student who files abiotic conditions under 'habitat' picks this. The guidance includes abiotic interactions, such as tolerance of temperature or oxygen, in the niche.

mcqs.q: Koalas (Phascolarctos cinereus) feed on Eucalyptus leaves, are active mainly at night, and are found in eucalypt woodland in eastern Australia where rainfall and temperature stay within particular ranges. Which statement about the ecological niche of the koala is correct?
options: Its niche is the eucalypt woodland of eastern Australia in which it lives and feeds
Its niche includes its Eucalyptus diet and its tolerance of rainfall and temperature
Its niche is fully described by its position as a primary consumer of leaves
Its niche includes its diet and its predators, but not the rainfall and temperature it tolerates
mcqs.specStatementText: Niche is a role, not a place
mcqs.explain: The niche is the role of the species, made up of biotic interactions such as feeding on Eucalyptus and abiotic interactions such as the ranges of rainfall and temperature it tolerates.
rationales: A student who treats the niche as a place picks this. The woodland is the koala's habitat; the niche is its role in that woodland.
The niche is the role of the species, made up of biotic interactions such as feeding on Eucalyptus and abiotic interactions such as the ranges of rainfall and temperature it tolerates.

A student who thinks the niche is only the trophic level picks this. Diet is part of the niche, but the abiotic conditions tolerated and interactions with predators and competitors are part of it too.
A student who keeps abiotic factors out of the niche picks this. The guidance includes abiotic interactions that influence growth, survival and reproduction in the niche.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes an obligate anaerobe?
options: An organism that does not use oxygen but is unharmed when oxygen gas is present
An organism that normally respires anaerobically but can use oxygen if needed
An organism that can grow only where oxygen gas is absent from its environment
An organism that switches to anaerobic respiration when its oxygen supply runs out
mcqs.explain: Obligate anaerobes cannot tolerate oxygen gas. They are found only in oxygen-free environments, such as deep sediments or the gut, because oxygen prevents their growth.
rationales: A student who pictures anaerobes as simply ignoring oxygen picks this. Oxygen is toxic to obligate anaerobes; they cannot tolerate it and grow only where it is absent.

A student who thinks the anaerobic mode is the organism's normal mode and oxygen is merely tolerated picks this. An organism that can use oxygen at all is a facultative anaerobe; an obligate anaerobe cannot tolerate oxygen.
Obligate anaerobes cannot tolerate oxygen gas. They are found only in oxygen-free environments, such as deep sediments or the gut, because oxygen prevents their growth.

A student who treats any organism that can respire without oxygen as an obligate anaerobe picks this. Switching between modes describes a facultative anaerobe; an obligate anaerobe never uses oxygen and cannot tolerate it.

mcqs.q: Three bacteria were cultured in liquid medium. Bacterium X grew only in a tube open to the air. Bacterium Y grew in both an open tube and a sealed oxygen-free tube, forming a denser culture in the open tube. Bacterium Z grew only in the sealed oxygen-free tube. Which classification is correct?
options: X obligate aerobe; Y obligate aerobe; Z obligate anaerobe, as Y grew better with oxygen
X obligate aerobe; Y obligate anaerobe; Z obligate anaerobe, as Y can grow without oxygen
X facultative anaerobe; Y facultative anaerobe; Z obligate anaerobe, as X could respire anaerobically
X obligate aerobe; Y facultative anaerobe; Z obligate anaerobe, by oxygen tolerance
mcqs.explain: Classification depends on tolerance of the presence or absence of oxygen. X tolerates only oxygen present (obligate aerobe), Y tolerates both (facultative anaerobe) and Z tolerates only oxygen absent (obligate anaerobe).
rationales: A student who reads 'obligate' as 'does best' picks this. Y grew without oxygen as well, so it does not require oxygen; growth in both conditions makes it a facultative anaerobe.
A student who thinks any organism able to grow without oxygen is an obligate anaerobe picks this. Y also grew with oxygen present, which an obligate anaerobe cannot do.
A student who assumes every organism can fall back on anaerobic respiration doubts that X truly needs oxygen. The data show X grew only with oxygen present, so it is an obligate aerobe.

Classification depends on tolerance of the presence or absence of oxygen. X tolerates only oxygen present (obligate aerobe), Y tolerates both (facultative anaerobe) and Z tolerates only oxygen absent (obligate anaerobe).

mcqs.q: In which groups of organisms is photosynthesis the mode of nutrition?
options: Plants, algae and several groups of photosynthetic prokaryotes such as cyanobacteria
Plants and algae only, because prokaryotes are unable to photosynthesize
Plants, algae and any prokaryotes whose cells happen to contain chloroplasts
Plants, algae and photosynthetic prokaryotes, though plants also feed from the soil
mcqs.specStatementText: Photosynthesis feeds plants, algae and some prokaryotes
mcqs.explain: Photosynthesis is the mode of nutrition of plants, of algae and of several groups of photosynthetic prokaryotes. All synthesize their own carbon compounds from carbon dioxide using light energy.
rationales: Photosynthesis is the mode of nutrition of plants, of algae and of several groups of photosynthetic prokaryotes. All synthesize their own carbon compounds from carbon dioxide using light energy.
A student who has met bacteria only as pathogens and decomposers picks this. Several groups of prokaryotes photosynthesize; the details of their types of photosynthesis are not required.
A student who ties photosynthesis to the chloroplast picks this. Prokaryotic cells have no chloroplasts, yet several groups of prokaryotes are photosynthetic.

A student who thinks plants take in food through their roots picks this. Plants absorb only water and mineral ions from the soil; all their carbon compounds are synthesized in photosynthesis, so this is not a second mode of nutrition.

mcqs.q: A dog eats meat. Proteins in the meat are hydrolysed in the gut, the amino acids pass across the wall of the small intestine into the blood, and later some of them are used in the dog's muscle cells to make new protein. Which term describes the use of the amino acids to make the dog's own protein?
options: Absorption, because the amino acids are being taken into the dog's tissues
Assimilation, because the products of digestion become part of the dog
Digestion, because it is the last step in the processing of the meat
Ingestion, because the amino acids are taken into the muscle cells
mcqs.explain: Holozoic nutrition ends with assimilation: absorbed products of digestion are taken up by cells and built into the animal's own molecules and tissues.
rationales: A student who treats absorption and assimilation as the same stage picks this. Absorption was the passage of amino acids across the gut wall into the blood; their use to build protein is a later stage.
Holozoic nutrition ends with assimilation: absorbed products of digestion are taken up by cells and built into the animal's own molecules and tissues.
A student who uses 'digestion' for everything the body does with food picks this. Digestion is the hydrolysis of proteins to amino acids, which happened in the gut before absorption.
A student who applies 'ingest' to uptake by cells picks this. Ingestion is the first stage, taking food into the body through the mouth; uptake by cells is part of assimilation.

mcqs.q: Which statement about nutrition in animals is correct?
options: Animals that host photosynthetic algae inside their cells are autotrophic
Animals assimilate their food by absorbing it across the lining of the gut
Animals are heterotrophs that ingest, digest, absorb and assimilate food
Animals ingest food when digested molecules pass into their cells
mcqs.explain: All animals are heterotrophic. Their holozoic nutrition consists of ingestion of food, internal digestion, absorption of the products and their assimilation into the animal's tissues.
rationales: A student who locates the mode of nutrition in the body rather than the organism picks this. The algae are autotrophs; the animal obtains carbon compounds from them and is heterotrophic.
A student who merges the two stages picks this. Passage across the gut wall is absorption; assimilation is the later use of the absorbed molecules in the animal's cells.
All animals are heterotrophic. Their holozoic nutrition consists of ingestion of food, internal digestion, absorption of the products and their assimilation into the animal's tissues.
A student who uses 'ingest' for uptake by cells picks this. Ingestion is taking food into the body at the start of holozoic nutrition, before digestion.

mcqs.q: Euglena gracilis is a freshwater protist with chloroplasts. Cultures grow in the light in a medium with no organic carbon compounds, and also grow in the dark when organic carbon compounds are supplied. Which statement about the nutrition of Euglena is correct?
options: It is an autotroph, because an organism with chloroplasts cannot also be a heterotroph
It is an obligate mixotroph, because it must photosynthesize whenever light is available
It is one of very few mixotrophs, because mixotrophy is confined to fresh water
It is a facultative mixotroph, because either mode alone can sustain it
mcqs.explain: Euglena grows by photosynthesis alone in the light and by heterotrophic nutrition alone in the dark. A mixotroph that can survive on one mode alone is facultative rather than obligate.
rationales: A student who thinks producer and consumer are exclusive categories picks this. Growth in the dark on organic compounds shows heterotrophic nutrition; Euglena uses both modes and is a mixotroph.
A student who attaches 'obligate' to photosynthesis picks this. An obligate mixotroph needs both modes at once; Euglena survives on either mode alone, so it is facultative.
A student who knows only the textbook example picks this. Euglena is the well-known freshwater example, but many mixotrophic species are part of oceanic plankton.
Euglena grows by photosynthesis alone in the light and by heterotrophic nutrition alone in the dark. A mixotroph that can survive on one mode alone is facultative rather than obligate.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes saprotrophic nutrition?
options: Secretion of enzymes onto dead organic matter, followed by absorption of the products of digestion
Ingestion of dead organic matter, followed by internal digestion and absorption of products
Any feeding on dead organic matter, whether by fungi and bacteria or by earthworms and woodlice
Synthesis of carbon compounds by fungi and bacteria that grow on dead organic matter
mcqs.explain: Saprotrophs such as many fungi and bacteria digest dead organic matter externally by secreting enzymes onto it and then absorb the soluble products. Organisms with this mode of nutrition can be referred to as decomposers.
rationales: Saprotrophs such as many fungi and bacteria digest dead organic matter externally by secreting enzymes onto it and then absorb the soluble products. Organisms with this mode of nutrition can be referred to as decomposers.
A student who applies the animal model of digestion to fungi picks this. Saprotrophs do not ingest; they digest externally and absorb the products.

A student who uses 'decomposer' loosely picks this. Earthworms and woodlice ingest dead matter and digest it internally; saprotrophic nutrition is specifically external digestion by fungi and bacteria.
A student who thinks of fungi as plant-like picks this. Fungi and saprotrophic bacteria are heterotrophs; they obtain carbon compounds from the dead matter rather than synthesizing them.

mcqs.q: Three species of archaea were studied. Species 1 obtains energy by oxidizing ammonia. Species 2 obtains energy by oxidizing carbon compounds absorbed from decaying matter. Species 3 obtains energy from light. What do these observations illustrate?
options: Archaea are a group of bacteria, so they show the same modes of nutrition as other bacteria
Archaea are metabolically diverse, using light, inorganic chemicals or carbon compounds
Archaea are chemosynthetic extremophiles, so only species 1 is a typical archaeon
Archaea are prokaryotes, so all three must be heterotrophs oxidizing carbon compounds
mcqs.specStatementText: Archaea: a domain of their own, metabolically diverse
mcqs.explain: The three species use the three energy sources named in the guidance: oxidation of an inorganic chemical (species 1), oxidation of a carbon compound (species 2) and light (species 3). Archaea are metabolically very diverse.
rationales: A student who still thinks of 'archaebacteria' picks this. Archaea are a separate domain of life from Bacteria; the observations illustrate diversity within that domain, not bacterial nutrition.

The three species use the three energy sources named in the guidance: oxidation of an inorganic chemical (species 1), oxidation of a carbon compound (species 2) and light (species 3). Archaea are metabolically very diverse.

A student who generalises from hot-spring examples picks this. All three are archaea; there is no single 'typical' archaeal metabolism, and many archaea live in ordinary soils and waters rather than extreme environments.
A student who thinks all prokaryotes are heterotrophic decomposers picks this. Only species 2 oxidizes carbon compounds; species 1 and 3 obtain energy from an inorganic chemical and from light.

mcqs.q: A skull of Paranthropus robustus, an extinct hominid, has very large flat molars with thick enamel, small incisors and canines, a massive lower jaw, and a sagittal crest along the top of the skull where large chewing muscles were attached. What can be deduced about its diet?
options: A diet of meat, since large jaw muscles indicate a powerful bite for seizing and killing prey
An omnivorous diet, since the presence of canines shows that some meat was eaten
A diet of tough plant material, since the teeth and jaw are adapted for prolonged grinding
Nothing reliable, since the diet of an extinct species cannot be inferred from its bones alone
mcqs.explain: Large flat molars with thick enamel, a massive jaw and a sagittal crest for big chewing muscles match the dentition of living herbivorous mammals that grind fibrous plant food, so a herbivorous diet is deduced.
rationales: A student who reads a robust skull as a predator's picks this. Meat is sheared with cutting teeth; large flat molars, thick enamel and heavy chewing muscles are for grinding tough plant material.
A student who treats canines as 'meat teeth' picks this. The canines here are small, and dentition must be read as a whole; the dominant features are the grinding molars and heavy jaw.

Large flat molars with thick enamel, a massive jaw and a sagittal crest for big chewing muscles match the dentition of living herbivorous mammals that grind fibrous plant food, so a herbivorous diet is deduced.
A student who accepts only direct observation picks this. Theories relating dentition to diet, built from living mammals, allow the diet of extinct species to be deduced from their skulls.

mcqs.q: How were biologists able to deduce the diets of extinct hominids such as Paranthropus robustus?
options: By developing theories relating dentition to diet from the fossils themselves, then confirming them with living mammals
By comparing the size of the fossil jaws with those of living carnivores, since powerful jaws indicate meat-eating
By treating the question as unanswerable, since the diet of an extinct animal is a guess that cannot be tested
By applying theories relating dentition to diet, developed from observing living mammals, to the fossil teeth
mcqs.explain: This is the NOS point: observation of living mammals led to theories relating dentition to herbivorous or carnivorous diets, and these theories allowed the diets of extinct organisms to be deduced.
rationales: A student who assumes the fossils supplied the theory picks this. The diets of fossil hominids were not observable, so the theory had to come from living mammals and was then applied to the fossils.

A student who equates a heavy jaw with carnivory picks this. In living mammals it is herbivores grinding tough plants that have massive jaws and large flat molars, so the comparison would be with herbivores.
A student who equates science with direct observation picks this. Deductions can be made from theories; the deduction can also be tested against other evidence such as tooth wear.
This is the NOS point: observation of living mammals led to theories relating dentition to herbivorous or carnivorous diets, and these theories allowed the diets of extinct organisms to be deduced.

mcqs.q: An aphid feeds on a leaf without removing any tissue, whereas a caterpillar leaves ragged holes in the leaf. Which statement explains the difference?
options: The aphid has piercing mouthparts that reach the sap, whereas the caterpillar has chewing mouthparts that bite off leaf tissue
Both insects have chewing mouthparts, but the aphid is so small that the holes it bites are too tiny to be seen
The aphid pierces the leaf to inject a toxin that digests the tissue, whereas the caterpillar chews the tissue
Leaves are soft and undefended, so neither insect needs special mouthparts; the aphid is too small to remove visible tissue
mcqs.explain: Leaf-eating insects have either piercing or chewing mouthparts. An aphid's stylets penetrate the leaf to feed on sap without removing tissue; a caterpillar's mandibles cut and chew pieces of leaf.
rationales: Leaf-eating insects have either piercing or chewing mouthparts. An aphid's stylets penetrate the leaf to feed on sap without removing tissue; a caterpillar's mandibles cut and chew pieces of leaf.
A student who assumes all leaf-eating insects chew picks this. Aphids do not bite; they have piercing mouthparts and feed on sap, which is why no tissue is removed.
A student who links piercing insects with injecting picks this. The aphid's piercing mouthparts are a feeding adaptation for reaching sap, not for injecting a toxin.

A student who thinks plants offer no resistance picks this. Leaves are tough and often toxic, and the two insects differ because they have different mouthparts, piercing stylets in the aphid and chewing mandibles in the caterpillar, not because of size.

mcqs.q: Koalas feed almost entirely on Eucalyptus leaves, which contain high concentrations of terpenes, secondary compounds produced by the plant. Which statement best explains how koalas survive on this diet?
options: Koalas have become immune to the terpenes, which no longer have any effect on their cells
Koalas have a metabolic adaptation: liver enzymes break the terpenes down for excretion
The terpenes are waste the leaf cannot excrete, so they have no real effect on animals
Terpenes deter insects but do not harm mammals, so koalas need no special adaptation
mcqs.explain: Some animals have metabolic adaptations for detoxifying plant toxins. Koalas have enzymes that chemically alter the terpenes into products that can be excreted, allowing them to eat a plant other mammals cannot.
rationales: A student who applies the everyday idea of immunity picks this. The terpenes still enter the koala's body; what differs is that the koala's metabolism chemically breaks them down.

Some animals have metabolic adaptations for detoxifying plant toxins. Koalas have enzymes that chemically alter the terpenes into products that can be excreted, allowing them to eat a plant other mammals cannot.
A student who thinks secondary compounds are stored waste picks this. Terpenes are toxic secondary compounds that resist herbivory; they poison most mammals that eat the leaves.
A student who generalises from grazing livestock picks this. Terpenes are toxic to most mammals; the koala is exceptional because of its detoxifying enzymes.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly classifies an adaptation as chemical, physical or behavioural, and as belonging to a predator or a prey animal?
options: A rattlesnake's venom is a physical adaptation of a predator, because it is injected through the fangs
Zebras living in herds is not an adaptation, because this behaviour is learned rather than inherited
A skunk spraying a foul-smelling secretion at an attacker is a chemical adaptation of a prey animal
A leopard's spotted coat cannot be a predator adaptation, because camouflage protects prey animals
mcqs.explain: The secretion is a chemical, and the skunk uses it to resist predation, so this is a chemical adaptation of a prey animal.
rationales: A student who classifies by the visible body part picks this. The fangs are a physical adaptation, but the venom itself is a chemical adaptation for killing prey.
A student who counts only anatomical features picks this. Herding is a behavioural adaptation of prey animals for resisting predation; it has a genetic basis and is shaped by natural selection.
The secretion is a chemical, and the skunk uses it to resist predation, so this is a chemical adaptation of a prey animal.
A student who has met camouflage only in prey picks this. Camouflage is also a physical adaptation of predators, allowing them to stalk or ambush prey unseen.

mcqs.q: Which pairing of a rainforest plant with its strategy for harvesting light is correct?
options: Liana: germinates on a high branch and grows roots down the trunk until they reach the soil
Epiphyte: absorbs water and carbon compounds from the xylem and phloem of the tree it grows on
Forest-floor herb: absorbs carbon compounds from decaying leaves instead of photosynthesizing
Strangler epiphyte: germinates high on a branch and later sends roots down to the soil
mcqs.specStatementText: Ways to reach the light in a forest
mcqs.explain: A strangler epiphyte starts life as an epiphyte, high up where light is available, and then grows roots down to the soil; as they thicken around the trunk and its crown shades the host, the host tree may die.
rationales: A student who confuses stranglers with climbers picks this. A liana is rooted in the soil and climbs up the tree; germinating high and rooting downwards is the strategy of a strangler epiphyte.
A student who thinks epiphytes are parasites picks this. Epiphytes use the branch only as a support to reach light; they photosynthesize for themselves and take water from rain.
A student who thinks plants cannot live in shade picks this. Shade-tolerant herbs photosynthesize at the low light intensities of the forest floor; they are not heterotrophs.

A strangler epiphyte starts life as an epiphyte, high up where light is available, and then grows roots down to the soil; as they thicken around the trunk and its crown shades the host, the host tree may die.

mcqs.q: Shrubs and herbs grow on the floor of a forest beneath a closed canopy. How do these plants obtain enough light to survive?
options: They are shade tolerant, able to photosynthesize at the low light intensities reaching the floor
They obtain carbon compounds from the decaying leaf litter, so they need little light
They receive sugar from the canopy trees through underground fungal networks
They cannot; plants that fail to reach the canopy survive only until they are shaded
mcqs.specStatementText: Ways to reach the light in a forest
mcqs.explain: Shade-tolerant shrubs and herbs are one of the strategies for harvesting light in forests: they are adapted to photosynthesize and complete their life cycle under the low light that reaches the forest floor.
rationales: Shade-tolerant shrubs and herbs are one of the strategies for harvesting light in forests: they are adapted to photosynthesize and complete their life cycle under the low light that reaches the forest floor.
A student who thinks plants cannot manage in shade picks this. Forest-floor herbs are autotrophs; they photosynthesize at low light intensity rather than feeding on litter.
A student influenced by popular accounts of the 'wood wide web' picks this. Shade-tolerant plants make their own carbon compounds by photosynthesis at low light intensities.
A student who sees a single race to the canopy picks this. Shade tolerance is a distinct strategy; these plants live their whole lives on the shaded forest floor.

mcqs.q: On a rocky shore, adult barnacles of one species (Chthamalus) are found only high on the shore, while a second species (Balanus) occupies the middle and lower shore. When Balanus was removed from areas of the middle and lower shore, Chthamalus settled, survived and grew there. What do these results show?
options: Chthamalus is absent from the lower shore because the physical conditions there are beyond its tolerance limits
The fundamental niche of Chthamalus includes the lower shore, but competition restricts its realized niche
The realized niche of Chthamalus is the whole shore and its fundamental niche is the upper shore
Removing Balanus caused Chthamalus to adapt so that it could tolerate lower-shore conditions
mcqs.explain: The removal experiment shows Chthamalus can tolerate the lower shore, so it lies within its fundamental niche. In the presence of Balanus its realized niche, the extent actually occupied, is restricted to the upper shore by competition.
rationales: A student who explains distribution by abiotic factors alone picks this. Chthamalus survived on the lower shore once Balanus was removed, so those conditions are within its tolerance.

The removal experiment shows Chthamalus can tolerate the lower shore, so it lies within its fundamental niche. In the presence of Balanus its realized niche, the extent actually occupied, is restricted to the upper shore by competition.
A student who inverts the two terms picks this. The fundamental niche is the potential (whole shore); the realized niche is the actual extent in competition (upper shore only).
A student who thinks tolerance changes in response to circumstances picks this. The tolerance limits of Chthamalus were unchanged; it occupied more of a fundamental niche it already had.

mcqs.q: Two species of Paramecium, P. aurelia and P. caudatum, both feed on bacteria. Grown in separate cultures with the same food supply, each species reached a stable population. Grown together in one culture, P. aurelia reached a similar density to when alone, while the population of P. caudatum declined steadily until almost none remained. Which conclusion is supported?
options: The two species would have reached a stable balance, sharing the bacteria, if the culture had been continued
P. aurelia eliminated P. caudatum by feeding on it, which is why the P. aurelia population stayed high
P. caudatum was excluded from the culture because the two species occupied exactly the same niche
P. caudatum became extinct as a species because P. aurelia is better adapted in all conditions
mcqs.explain: With identical food and conditions the two species had the same niche, and competitive exclusion followed: the species that used the bacteria more effectively persisted and the other was eliminated from the culture.
rationales: A student who expects similar species to share picks this. The data show P. caudatum declining steadily to almost nothing, not levelling off; two species with the same niche cannot coexist indefinitely.
A student who imagines competition as a fight picks this. Both species feed on bacteria and neither eats the other; P. caudatum declined because P. aurelia used the shared food more effectively.

With identical food and conditions the two species had the same niche, and competitive exclusion followed: the species that used the bacteria more effectively persisted and the other was eliminated from the culture.

A student who reads elimination as extinction picks this. P. caudatum was eliminated only from this culture; it persists wherever its realized niche does not overlap completely with a superior competitor.

mcqs.q: The fundamental niches of two species overlap and the two species compete. What are the possible outcomes?
options: Both species continue to occupy their whole fundamental niches, sharing the resources between them
The species that loses is driven to extinction throughout its range, wherever it occurs
The stronger species eliminates the weaker by preying on it until none remains in the area
One species is eliminated, or both are restricted to part of their fundamental niche
mcqs.explain: The guidance gives exactly these two outcomes. Either competitive exclusion removes one species from the area, or each species is confined to a realized niche that is only part of its fundamental niche.
rationales: A student who expects coexisting species to share picks this. Where niches overlap, competition either eliminates one species or restricts both to part of their fundamental niches.

A student who equates exclusion with extinction picks this. Elimination is from the area of competition; the species can persist elsewhere or in parts of its fundamental niche the competitor does not use.
A student who confuses competition with predation picks this. Competitors do not eat each other; one species is eliminated because the other uses the shared resource more effectively.

The guidance gives exactly these two outcomes. Either competitive exclusion removes one species from the area, or each species is confined to a realized niche that is only part of its fundamental niche.

mcqs.q: Two hominid skulls are compared. Skull A has very large flat molars with thick enamel, small canines, a massive lower jaw and a sagittal crest for large chewing muscles. Skull B has relatively small molars, small canines little larger than the incisors, a lighter jaw and no sagittal crest. What can be deduced about the diets of the two species?
options: A was herbivorous, grinding tough plant material; B was omnivorous, with unspecialised teeth suited to a mixed diet
A was carnivorous, because a massive jaw and crest indicate a powerful killing bite; B was herbivorous
Both were carnivorous, because both skulls have canine teeth, which are the teeth used for tearing meat
Nothing can be deduced about the diet of either species, because neither of them can be observed feeding
mcqs.explain: Large flat molars, a massive jaw and a crest match living herbivores that grind fibrous plants; small unspecialised teeth with reduced canines match living omnivores such as Homo sapiens, so A is deduced to be herbivorous and B omnivorous.
rationales: Large flat molars, a massive jaw and a crest match living herbivores that grind fibrous plants; small unspecialised teeth with reduced canines match living omnivores such as Homo sapiens, so A is deduced to be herbivorous and B omnivorous.

A student who reads a massive jaw and crest as a predator's picks this. Meat is sheared by cutting teeth; heavy chewing muscles and large flat molars are for grinding tough plant food, so A was herbivorous and B, with unspecialised teeth, omnivorous.

A student who treats canines as 'meat teeth' picks this. Almost all mammals have canines; dentition must be read as a whole, and neither skull has the large pointed canines and shearing teeth of a carnivore.
A student who accepts only direct observation picks this. Theories relating dentition to diet, developed from living mammals, allow the diets of both extinct species to be deduced from their skulls.

specStatements.text: Niche is a role, not a place
Photosynthesis feeds plants, algae and some prokaryotes
Archaea: a domain of their own, metabolically diverse
Ways to reach the light in a forest

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Obligate anaerobes, facultative anaerobes and obligate aerobes are distinguished only by whether they can grow with oxygen present, with oxygen absent, or both. No item, concept or misconception requires the biochemistry of oxygen toxicity, the enzymes involved, aerotolerant or microaerophilic categories, or named example species.

Photosynthetic prokaryotes are treated only as groups that use photosynthesis as their mode of nutrition. Nothing is included on oxygenic versus anoxygenic photosynthesis, bacteriochlorophylls, or the pigments and electron donors used by different prokaryote groups.

Archaea are treated as one of the three domains and as metabolically diverse, using light, oxidation of inorganic chemicals or oxidation of carbon compounds as energy sources for ATP production. No item asks students to name or recognise a genus or species of archaea; where an item describes an archaeon it is referred to only as 'an archaeon' or 'species 1'.
